Continually fine-tuned classifiers face a specific failure mode: as you adapt a model sequentially to new domains, the model's confidence scores decouple from its actual accuracy — it stays roughly calibrated on held-out test sets from each new domain, but the calibration on earlier domains silently degrades, often without triggering any alarm in standard evaluation pipelines. The central question is whether this degradation is an unavoidable consequence of shifting the decision boundary (which necessarily reshapes the softmax geometry) or whether it can be mitigated without full replay of earlier domain data. Key concepts include Expected Calibration Error (ECE) as a function of training stage, temperature scaling's fragility under distribution shift, the distinction between discriminative recalibration (adjusting the boundary) and probabilistic recalibration (adjusting confidence given a fixed boundary), and the difference between catastrophic forgetting of labels versus catastrophic forgetting of uncertainty structure. What a beginner misses is that a classifier can maintain high accuracy on all domains simultaneously while its calibration collapses — the network learns to be confidently wrong on boundary cases from earlier domains, because nothing in the cross-entropy loss penalizes overconfidence on correctly-classified examples. The expert worry is subtler still: post-hoc recalibration methods like temperature scaling learn a single scalar from a validation set, but under sequential adaptation the optimal temperature is domain-dependent and non-stationary, so a global recalibration applied after training systematically underestimates uncertainty at domain boundaries where the model has been fine-tuned most recently.

Under sequential fine-tuning, this effect compounds: the new domain's gradient updates push the softmax logits toward higher-magnitude outputs (a known consequence of weight norm growth during fine-tuning), which inflates confidence globally, and earlier-domain examples get swept along into higher-confidence bins without any corresponding accuracy gain. The ratio does shift with domain distance, but not symmetrically — when the new domain is close in feature space (e.g., adapting a medical imaging classifier from one hospital's scanner to another's), the earlier domain's misclassified examples actually gain slightly better-calibrated uncertainty because the decision boundary moves only locally; the overconfidence on correct examples still worsens. When the new domain is far (e.g., adapting from chest X-rays to dermatology, as studied in continual learning benchmarks like Split-CUB or sequential medical imaging setups), both failure modes appear, but overconfidence still dominates numerically in ECE because misclassified examples are fewer in absolute count. The practical implication is grim: since standard early stopping and validation loss monitoring don't observe calibration directly, this overconfidence accumulates silently across adaptation steps until it materializes as unreliable downstream decisions.

The analogy is to curriculum learning, where ordering examples by difficulty improves convergence, but here the ordering operates on the output layer's degrees of freedom rather than the input distribution; when well-aligned class heads are unfrozen first and allowed to stabilize, they effectively regularize the loss landscape that misaligned heads must navigate when they're subsequently released.
